title: Lock Escalation: One Big Update Locks the Whole Table
description: A single huge UPDATE escalates to a table lock and blocks an unrelated row; batching it under the escalation threshold keeps locks fine-grained. Why it matters: batch jobs and bulk updates are routine in production, and lock escalation is a common, invisible way they end up blocking completely unrelated user traffic.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine a library that normally lets you check out individual books one at a time, tracked book-by-book. But if you try to check out an enormous number of books in one visit, at some point the librarian decides tracking each individual book is too much bookkeeping, and instead just locks the entire room you're browsing in, telling everyone else "nobody else can come in here until this person is done" — even though you only actually wanted a fraction of the books in that room. This lesson is about SQL Server doing exactly that: automatically switching from fine-grained, per-row locking to one big, coarse lock, once an operation touches enough rows.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** Lock escalation is SQL Server's automatic behavior of converting many individual row-level (or page-level) locks into a single, much broader table-level lock, once the number of individual locks held by one statement crosses a threshold. This lesson is about what triggers that escalation, and about the very real, sometimes surprising collateral damage it causes to completely unrelated queries.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Every individual lock SQL Server holds costs a small amount of memory to track. That's a perfectly reasonable cost when a handful of locks are involved, but if a single statement — a large batch update, a bulk delete, a big data-fixing script — ends up needing tens of thousands of individual row locks, the memory overhead of tracking every single one of them individually starts to add up in a way SQL Server considers wasteful. Rather than let that overhead grow without bound, SQL Server has a built-in safety valve: past a certain number of locks held by one statement (by default, around 5,000), it automatically escalates, replacing all those individual fine-grained locks with one single table-level lock that covers everything at once, dramatically cutting the memory overhead — at the direct cost of losing the fine-grained precision of "only this row is locked."

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Picture a large `UPDATE` statement, running inside a transaction, that ends up needing to touch, say, 50,000 rows across a big table — maybe a batch job correcting a data issue across many rows at once. As it works through those rows, SQL Server is acquiring an exclusive lock per row (or sometimes per page) as it goes, and it's tracking every one of those locks individually in memory. Once the number of locks held by this single statement crosses the escalation threshold, SQL Server makes a decision: rather than continue accumulating tens of thousands of individual locks, it takes out one exclusive lock on the entire table and releases (or simply stops tracking) all the fine-grained locks it had been holding, since the one table-level lock now covers everything anyway. From that moment until this transaction commits or rolls back, *nobody else* can touch *any* row in that table — not just the rows the update actually needed, but every single row in the entire table, including rows the update was never going to touch in the first place, and including rows some completely unrelated query somewhere else in the application might urgently need right now.

**Why this matters in production.** Batch jobs, bulk updates, and large data-correction scripts are routine in real production systems, and they're exactly the kind of operation that touches enough rows to trigger escalation. The surprising and often infuriating part is the collateral damage: once escalation kicks in, an update that logically only cares about, say, "all orders placed last Tuesday" ends up blocking every single other query touching that table — including a completely unrelated customer trying to look up their own single order that the batch job was never even going to touch — for as long as the whole batch transaction takes to finish. This produces a confusing symptom in production: a big background job runs, and suddenly unrelated, small, simple queries elsewhere in the application start timing out or hanging, with no apparent connection between the two, until you know to look specifically for a table-level lock caused by escalation as the hidden link.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is to keep the number of rows touched, and therefore the number of locks needed, *under* the escalation threshold in the first place — typically by breaking one enormous update into a loop of smaller batches (say, a few thousand rows at a time), each running and committing as its own separate, smaller transaction. Because each individual batch stays under the threshold, escalation never triggers, locks stay fine-grained and row-level throughout, and unrelated queries touching other rows in the same table are free to proceed the entire time the batch job is running, rather than being frozen out by one giant, table-wide lock.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs one large update that crosses the escalation threshold, and shows you a completely unrelated query against a different row in the same table getting blocked by the resulting table-level lock. After rewriting the update to run in smaller batches that each stay under the threshold, re-run the same interleaving and watch the unrelated query proceed freely the whole time, because no single batch ever accumulates enough locks to trigger escalation into one table-wide lock.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** The default escalation threshold (roughly 5,000 locks) can be adjusted or disabled per table via `ALTER TABLE ... SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = ...)`, but changing that setting is a blunt instrument that should be considered carefully rather than reached for automatically — disabling escalation entirely removes the memory-overhead safety valve escalation exists to provide, and can itself cause problems on a server under real memory pressure. Batching large operations to naturally stay under the threshold is almost always the safer, more broadly applicable fix, and it has the added benefit of making each batch's own transaction shorter, which independently reduces ordinary blocking too.

It's also worth checking whether an update genuinely needs to run as one single transaction at all — if the business logic allows each batch to commit independently rather than needing all-or-nothing atomicity across the entire operation, batching is both safer for concurrency and easier to resume cleanly if the job is interrupted partway through.

## Scenario
A nightly job (Session A) posts interest to 40,000 ledger rows inside one transaction. Meanwhile Session B just wants to correct **one** unrelated row at the far end of the table. B hangs until the batch job commits — even though the two never touch the same rows.

## Why it blocks
SQL Server starts with fine-grained **row/page locks**, but once a single statement acquires roughly **5,000 locks** it trades them all for one coarse **table lock** — this is **lock escalation**. A's 40,000-row `UPDATE` sails past that threshold and takes an exclusive lock on the *entire* `Ledger` table. Now B's update of row 49,999 can't get even a single row lock, because the whole table is locked. B blocks for the full duration of A's transaction.

## What to look for
- A's `UPDATE` shows a table-level `X` lock (escalated), not thousands of row locks.
- B is blocked waiting on an **object-level** lock it should never have needed.

## The concept
Keep any one statement under the escalation threshold so it never grabs the table. **Batch** the work — update in chunks of ~2,000 rows, each committing on its own — so A only ever holds a handful of locks at a time and B's unrelated row stays free. (The blunt alternative is `ALTER TABLE Ledger SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE)`, but batching also shortens how long any lock is held.)
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Rewrite Session A's giant UPDATE to run in batches, then Run the interleaving.
hints: B is blocked on a table-level lock, but it only wants one row. Something made A lock the whole table.
A single statement that locks ~5,000+ rows escalates to one table lock. A's UPDATE hits 40,000 rows in one shot.
Split A's UPDATE into batches under the threshold, each auto-committing: WHILE loop doing UPDATE ... WHERE LedgerId BETWEEN @i AND @i+1999; so it never escalates.

interleaving.description: Session A updates 40,000 rows in one transaction and escalates to a table lock; Session B's single-row update on an unrelated row blocks behind it.

A.sql: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE Ledger SET Amount = Amount + 1 WHERE LedgerId <= 40000;

B.sql: UPDATE Ledger SET Amount = Amount + 5 WHERE LedgerId = 49999;

interleaving.solutionNote: Rewrite A's single 40,000-row UPDATE into a WHILE loop that updates ~2,000 rows per iteration and auto-commits each batch, so no statement ever reaches the ~5,000-lock escalation threshold. A then only holds a few locks at a time and B's unrelated row (49999) is never blocked. Alternatively ALTER TABLE Ledger SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE).
